settings.copy: Meridian Point is a working public observatory perched above the valley. On clear nights we open the dome, aim the big telescope, and hand the eyepiece to whoever's next in line. No astronomy degree required — just curiosity and a warm coat.

settings.title: How a clear night
settings.intro: Every open night follows the same patient rhythm — from the first glimpse of the sky to the last look before the dome closes. Here's what happens when you come up the ridge.

steps.title: Arrive as the light fades
steps.text: You park at the ridge and walk up as the sky deepens. We meet you at the door, hand you a warm drink, and let your eyes adjust to the dark before the dome opens.

steps.title: Tour the sky by eye
steps.text: Before the telescope, we point out the constellations, the planets, and the satellites crossing overhead — a guided tour of the sky you can see with nothing but your own eyes.

steps.title: Look through the big scope
steps.text: The 20-inch telescope swings into position and we aim it at the night's best targets. Saturn's rings, the craters of the Moon, a nebula that looks like a photograph — you get the eyepiece and time to really look.

steps.title: Ask anything
steps.text: Our astronomers stay until the last visitor leaves. Bring your questions, your kids, or your own telescope for a second opinion. The dome closes when the sky does, not on a schedule.

settings.note: Meridian Point is built on patience: if clouds roll in, we don't call it a wasted night — we run the indoor planetarium show and reschedule your telescope time for the next clear evening.

settings.title: A place built
settings.intro: There are closer places to see the stars, but none that do it like this. Here's what makes a night at the ridge worth the drive.

features.title: A genuinely dark sky
features.text: We sit above the valley's light dome, on a ridge where the Milky Way is visible on clear nights. The darkness is the whole point — and we protect it.

features.title: A serious telescope
features.text: Our 20-inch reflector gathers enough light to show you Saturn's rings, the bands of Jupiter, and nebulae that look like photographs. It's the real thing.

features.title: Astronomers, not scripts
features.text: The people at the eyepiece are working astronomers who love to talk. They'll answer the question you were too shy to ask — and the one you didn't know you had.

features.title: Open every clear night
features.text: No seasonal schedule, no 'closed for the month.' If the sky is clear, the dome is open — all year, rain or shine (well, shine).

features.title: Built for wonder
features.text: Kids get their own step stool at the eyepiece and their own patient guide. We've seen a hundred first-time 'whoa's — and we never get tired of them.

features.title: A planetarium for cloudy nights
features.text: When the sky won't cooperate, the indoor dome takes over with a full-sky show. You still get a night of astronomy — just under a different roof.

settings.title: The moment the
settings.intro: People come up the ridge expecting a look at the stars and leave with a story. Here's a little of what they tell us on the way back down.

reviews.quote: I've seen Saturn's rings in photos my whole life. Seeing them through that telescope, with my own eye, was genuinely one of the best moments of my year. The astronomer didn't rush me at all.
reviews.author: Dana Whitfield

reviews.quote: We brought our two kids expecting twenty minutes of patience. They stayed two hours, asked a hundred questions, and talked about the nebula for a week. Worth every minute of the drive.
reviews.author: Tom & Aisha Grant

reviews.quote: I brought my own small telescope for a second opinion and the astronomer spent half an hour helping me collimate it. The sky up there is unreal — the Milky Way is actually visible.
reviews.author: Ravi Menon
